name: The Prince
kicker: Machiavelli’s 1513 guide for rulers · How to seize and keep power
briefing: After losing his government job in 1512, a Florentine diplomat named Niccolò Machiavelli wrote a blunt how-to guide for rulers in 1513, hoping to win back a position. Instead of preaching about how rulers should be good, it coolly explained how rulers actually keep power — arguing that a prince should act like both a lion and a fox, and that it is safer to be feared than loved.

sample.note: 4 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One chapter of this work contrasts the military styles of Hannibal and Scipio Africanus to discuss cruelty versus mercy in leadership. A chapter on flatterers describes Emperor Maximilian I as a secretive ruler who kept changing his plans. This treatise also warns rulers against relying on hired mercenaries instead of their own citizen soldiers.
tossups.r: This work advises a ruler to combine the cunning of a fox with the strength of a lion. For 10 points, name this political treatise claiming that it is better for a ruler to be feared than loved, written by Niccolò Machiavelli.

tossups.p: This book was placed on the Catholic Church’s Index of Forbidden Books in 1559 for its blunt, nonreligious advice. Its author’s own surname later gave English an adjective describing cunning, deceptive political scheming. This work contrasts a ruler’s own skill, or virtù, with fortuna, the unpredictable force of luck.
tossups.r: Dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici, this work is best known for arguing that it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli.

tossups.p: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote this work after losing his government post when the Medici family retook Florence in 1512, hoping it would win him a new job. Years earlier, as a diplomat, he had personally met Cesare Borgia, whom this work later holds up as a model ruler. This work sorts states into types, including those won by one’s own arms and those won through fortune.
tossups.r: It is often summed up by the saying that the ends justify the means. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Machiavelli.

tossups.p: This work warns that a ruler who is too generous will eventually need to raise taxes and will be resented for it anyway. It also claims that people will promise their “blood, property, life, and children” when no real sacrifice is actually required of them. Its author also wrote an unrelated comic play, _La Mandragola_.
tossups.r: Dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici, this work urges a ruler to act like both a lion and a fox. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli.

tossups.p: Written around 1513 but not published until 1532, five years after its author’s death, this work is considered a founding text of political realism, since it studies how rulers actually behave rather than how they ought to behave. It uses Cesare Borgia as its central example of a ruler who seized power through calculated ruthlessness.
tossups.r: This work is famous for arguing that the ends justify the means and that it is better to be feared than loved. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli.

tossups.p: This work divides states into hereditary principalities, new ones won by one’s own arms or by fortune, and ones ruled by the Church. Because of its blunt, nonreligious advice, this work later landed on the Catholic Church’s Index of Forbidden Books.
tossups.r: It contrasts a ruler’s own skill, or virtù, with fortuna, the unpredictable force of luck, and advises combining the cunning of a fox with the strength of a lion. For 10 points, name this political treatise claiming it is better to be feared than loved, written by Niccolò Machiavelli.

tossups.p: Its author met Cesare Borgia in person while serving as a Florentine diplomat, an experience that shaped this work’s portrait of Borgia as a model ruler. The author’s own surname later became an English adjective for cunning, deceptive scheming in politics.
tossups.r: Dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici, this work is often summed up by the saying that the ends justify the means. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli.

trap.title: The book, or its author?
trap.body: Real tossup packets have separate answer lines for this book and for its author, Niccolò Machiavelli — a search for one often turns up tossups on the other. A question built around a single text (“this work,” “this treatise,” “this book”) wants the title. One covering a whole career, a different book, or personal biography wants Machiavelli himself.
trap.fix: Machiavelli-the-person clues: his other book _Discourses on Livy_, his comic play _La Mandragola_, his years as a Florentine diplomat, and his torture by the Medici. This-work clues: the lion and the fox, Cesare Borgia as an example ruler, and the dedication to Lorenzo de’ Medici.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Prince (or Il Principe)
